# Leaking Fuel Injector Seal

Removing fuel injectors and the fuel rail for EGR port cleaning is a standard maintenance procedure, but it frequently exposes latent sealing issues that weren't apparent when the system was pressurized or cold. In your specific case, replacing all O-rings, cushion rings, and injector seals with fresh parts should have resolved the vacuum leak, yet one seal continues to fail. The symptomsâa high idle ranging from 1.5 to 2k RPM that worsens after brakingâare classic indicators of an unmetered air intake entering the engine via a compromised cylinder head gasket or injector seal.

The core issue lies in the geometry of the sealing surface. You noted that part of the metal on the engine block where the injector seats isn't perfectly even. In automotive engineering, "flatness" is critical for high-pressure seals. Even microscopic imperfections can break the seal under low pressure but allow air to ingress once the system is under vacuum or fluctuating load conditions. The fact that the problem persists after replacing OEM-style seals suggests the sealing surface itself has degraded, likely due to thermal expansion cycles or improper torque on the fuel rail bolts during reassembly.

Applying clean oil or silicone gasket maker around the injector seal, as you attempted, is a temporary workaround that masks the root cause rather than fixing it. Oil can swell rubber slightly, creating a momentary seal, but once the oil drains or evaporates, the leak returns. Similarly, using RTV (Room Temperature Vulcanizing) silicone spray in an attempt to fill gaps introduces significant risks. Silicone cures over time, becoming brittle and potentially cracking under the thermal cycling of an engine. Furthermore, if the silicone migrates into the injector nozzle or fuel rail, it can contaminate the injectors themselves, leading to poor atomization and rough running conditions unrelated to the vacuum leak.

The idea of using a heavier weight engine oil is also a misconception. The viscosity of the lubricant does not dictate the sealing capability of an O-ring or cushion ring in this application; the seal relies on the compression set of the rubber against the metal face. Adding a washer in front of the cushion ring to increase pressure is dangerous. Over-compressing a fuel injector cushion ring can permanently deform the elastomer, causing it to lose its ability to return to shape and eventually leading to a complete seal failure or damage to the injector O-ring groove.

The most effective solution for an uneven sealing surface is to replace the compromised metal component rather than patching it with sealant. In many Honda Accord models, the fuel rail seats directly into a machined surface on the cylinder head that can warp or develop imperfections over time. If this surface is uneven, installing new seals will not suffice because the contact area remains insufficient.

If machining the block to correct the flatness is not feasible due to cost or access, the only reliable path forward is to install a dedicated fuel rail gasket between the rail and the head that covers the uneven area, provided there is enough clearance on the cylinder head surface. If the unevenness is on the injector itself, replacing the specific injector with a unit verified to have a smooth sealing face is necessary.

There are no aftermarket chemical sealants robust enough for high-temperature fuel system applications that can permanently fix an uneven metal-to-metal interface in this context. The persistent vacuum leak causing your idle surge indicates that air is being drawn into the intake manifold through the injector bore. This must be addressed by ensuring a perfect mating surface between the fuel rail and the cylinder head, or by replacing the specific injector with one that has a pristine sealing face. Continuing to rely on oils or sealants in this scenario risks damaging the fuel injectors or introducing debris into the combustion chamber.
